subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which was originally brought to the attention of the House yesterday by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). A minister of the Crown has made statements, or it has been claimed that he has made statements which are clearly racist and discriminatory in nature and which, if true, put this parliament and all its members under the cloud of racism.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in this House yesterday the minister in question denied that he said what was attributed to him. Subsequently, outside the House, however, the author of the article in question, who is herself an associate editor of Maclean's magazine, asserted that the minister not only made the statement attributed to him in her article, of which she has records, but made others even more damaging which were not included in the article. Mr. Speaker, if you agree there is a prima facie question of privilege, I would move:
That this matter be referred immediately to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that both the minister and the author of the article can appear to clarify this most serious question.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege, I thought I had made it clear to the House yesterday that I personally regretted the words that were used in that article just as much as the member for Yukon regrets those words-

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE
speechtext:
The member for Northwest
Territories.

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE
speechtext: I meant the Northwest Territories. But the words are not mine. The words did not express my sentiments. They did not express my feelings about the native people of this country. I said that in the House, I said it last night on television and I repeat that today. I can produce other statements I have made in which I said it is my hope that we can achieve a better life for the original Canadians, the native people of this country, within our society. Those statements reflect my true sentiments. That article, to which reference has been made, does not reflect my sentiments and I repudiate the statement as being mine.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE
speechtext: The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has put forward what he suggests is a question of privilege. I cannot emphasize too strongly, of course, the seriousness of the matter with which the hon. member is dealing. However, the type of statement complained of does not, in my opinion, come under any of the definitions of privilege as I understand them. I do not want to discuss what other approaches may be taken if the hon. member feels that the matter should be dealt with further. But it does not, in my opinion, come within the confines of any definition of privilege, as I understand that. In any case, for the second time the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) has denied categorically responsibility for the statement and, therefore, there does not seem to be anything further that the Chair can do about the question of privilege at this time.

I was tempted to speak on the question of privilege just raised but felt that the matter might better be covered by a motion moved under Standing Order 43. I find the alleged statements particularly disturbing, as I know that many native people, not only in my constituency but from all over Canada, have distinguished themselves in our armed forces in the defence of our country. I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the President of the Treasury Board about his position on strikes in the public service now under way among the general trades and labour group arises from the fact that a good many Canadians in business, as well as others, are being seriously hurt or inconvenienced by the continuation of the strike. The Minister indicated he did not propose to budge beyond the position taken by the majority of the conciliation board. How long does the minister intend to maintain his position and let this strike continue? Can the minister indicate how long the strike will continue so that those people being inconvenienced or hurt will try to make some alternative arrangements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how long the strike will last. I am happy to say that this morning the people at Terminal A in Toronto returned to work. There is some inconvenience when there is a strike, but the right to strike has been given to these employees by the parliament of Canada. I respect that right. At the same time, I think we have come a long way. I hope the union will recognize that the conciliation report was made by an outsider who, in fact, tried to offer them a fair deal. That is my position. I hope that talks will be resumed in order to try to find an acceptable solution. However, if they do not want to

return to work, I do not intend to introduce legislation to that effect at this time. I respect the right that all members of parliament have given to those employees.

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: The minister has made it clear he is not prepared to bargain with regard to his position. I am not necessarily criticizing the minister for that. However, the minister having taken that position, in his judgment what is the point of continuing? Is this simply a war of attrition between the government and the unions with the people of Canada, in the middle, getting hurt? How long is this war of attrition going to continue? With the minister taking the firm position he has, what meaning does the right to strike have in these circumstances?

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know how long the strike will last. The employees are entitled to strike. I maintain and repeat that the Treasury Board and the government have not been adamant, on the contrary. We had made some proposals which were quite lower than those suggested by the mediator and we have been willing to meet the mediator's requirements. We are ready to negotiate on the basis of that report. I hope the union will recognize that we have done our share and that they should do theirs and consider the report as a satisfactory basis for agreement. My conciliators are ready to meet the union at any time.

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Do I take it that the minister is in fact prepared to negotiate and that his position is not the apparently rigid position that he announced? Is he in fact prepared to negotiate? What steps are being taken to have negotiations reopened so that some progress can be made and the strike does not appear to be meaningless with the minister refusing to give any ground, if that is his position?

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS- POSSIBLE LENGTH OF STRIKE-WILLINGNESS OF MINISTER TO RE-OPEN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said that my conciliators are willing to meet with the union any time. They invited the union to meet with them these last few days, but the union did not think fit to do so. I hope consultations will soon resume, because we are prepared to settle the dispute. Far from having been rigid, on the contrary we have been very flexible, but we believe the conciliation report represents a good basis for settlement. I hope the union will consider this position as being a considerable improvement over what the government offered at the beginning of the negotiations.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
My supplementary is for the Postmaster General. It relates to the situa-
February 28, 1975

tion in the Toronto terminal-we are pleased to hear the employees are back on the job there. Arising from reports that truckers have refused and are refusing to cross the picket lines in Toronto because of threats of tire slashing and other acts of violence from the ideological element which is a small minority in the Tronto Post Office, and in view of the expressed desire of the majority of the workers there to stay on the job, what steps are being taken to weed out these bad apples?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Perhaps I could expand my answer in order to be more precise. The couriers or truck drivers were notified by me as Postmaster General that if they respected picket lines which were informational picket lines on philosophical grounds, that was their right, but the Canadian public was not to suffer because of their philosophy and if they refused to cross informational picket lines they would be suspended and replaced by drivers who did not necessarily share that basic philosophy.
As to the second question relating to violence on trucks to which the hon. gentleman quite properly referred, the violence occurred during the evening when the trucks were in the care of a private protection agency which has since been charged with negligence. There is no evidence that the damage to the trucks was caused by radical elements in the union; it could have been caused by radical groups outside the union. The point is that the truckers cannot have it both ways-respect picket lines on philosophical grounds and expect the Canadian public to suffer financial losses as a result of their conception of what is right and wrong.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext: In view of the concern expressed by the president of the postal union which resulted in his absence from the Finkelman committee yesterday, is there any possibility of a rapprochement with the union to deal with the tendency toward violence in the Toronto strike situation?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext: There is another and not unrelated issue and that is the negotiations within the Post Office itself. When I assumed the role of Postmaster General eight months ago my aim was to increase the efficiency of the Post Office by improving the morale of the workers, by introducing some form of industrial democracy at plant level and by reducing the unintentional interference of other departments of government. I had presumed I would get the co-operation of the union leaders who should be seeking the same thing. When the president of the union on one hand cancels an appearance yesterday before a committee of the House in order to go to Toronto on the ground that he has to prevent violence and at the same time issues a circular or bulletin inciting violence to begin, one wonder whether the leaders are working in the best interest of the members.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
When you add to this the fact that the union negotiating team has placed certain prerequisites before me, through our joint negotiating team-the Treasury Board and the Post Office-before they will sit down and bargain on behalf of the workers, conditions which are impossible such as that we become a Crown corpora-

tion, that we give them retroactive money, that we prevent all automation during negotiations, conditions which are impossible, it is obvious they have no intention of bargaining in good faith and the people who will ultimately lose by this are the 98 per cent of the postal workers who are basically decent, honest Canadians who simply want to get on with the job.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AND ELIMINATE THOSE EMPLOYEES WHO USE VIOLENCE

subsubtopic: ALLEGED RACIAL SLUR ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE-SUGGESTED REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. Yesterday in the House, in reply to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Northwest Territories concerning the quotation that was attributed to him in Maclean's magazine, the minister said as reported at page 3628 of Hansard:
There was no quotation by me in those terms.
I ask the minister-and I choose my words with care-is he saying, when he said that, that he did not say the following sentences even in a context which was somewhat different but which were run together in paragraph form, with reference to Canada's native people:
I mean, what did they even do for Canada? Did they discover gas? Did they discover oil? They didn't even invent the wheel. Why, when we came here, they were still dragging things around on two sticks.
Did the minister or did he not utter any of those sentences?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED RACIAL SLUR ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE IN "MACLEAN'S" MAGAZINE-SUGGESTED REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not utter those words in any way resembling the sentiment that is expressed in those words. I talked again last night with the author of the article and she admitted to me that we had not discussed native people, or my views of native people, in any way during our interview. She said that while we were talking of the Mackenzie valley pipeline I had made some remarks about the fact that American companies had helped develop Canadian oil, and that some of us in Canada had walked over the oil for a long time. But that was not directed toward native people. I repeat that the whole quotation is completely out of context. We were not talking about native people, according to the author, at the time that she made this report. What I am trying to tell the House is that those are not my feelings or my sentiments in any way. In fact quite the opposite.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE REPRESENTATION AND ESTABLISH A COMMISSION TO READJUST ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-51, to increase the representation of the Northwest Territories in the House of Commons and to establish a commission to readjust the electoral boundaries of the Northwest Territories, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide an additional representative for the Northwest Territories in the House of Commons, commencing with the next parliament, and to establish a means of dividing the Northwest Territories into two electoral districts. More generally, the bill is intended to complete the process begun with the Representation Act, 1974, of according equitable representation in the House of Commons to all provinces and territories of Canada, and to complement Bill C-3 which provides for representation in the Senate for the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory in giving a greater voice in parliament to the territories.
The present constituency of the Northwest Territories is unique in Canada today. Its outstanding feature is, of course, its immense size; its area covers over 1,300,000 square miles and is far greater than one member of parliament can physically be expected to visit and to be thoroughly acquainted with. Communications and transportation difficulties add to the problems faced by the member for the Northwest Territories despite considerable advances in recent years.
Members are well acquainted with recent economic and social developments in the north which have been rapidly expanding the role of the Northwest Territories in the life of the Canadian nation. These developments have been accompanied by accelerated population growth. The population of the Northwest Territories was approximately 16,000 when the original constituency of Mackenzie River first came into existence in 1952, and was recently estimated by Statistics Canada to be 38,000 in July, 1974. This is double the estimate for the Yukon territory. Finally, it is well to remember the special federal presence within the Northwest Territories and the special federal role in the development and government of the Northwest Territories.
Many proposals for the division of the Northwest Territories into two constituencies have been studied by the government, including those suggested by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) in private members' bills. Cultural and economic kinship among the people of the eastern and western regions, as well as geographical differences between east and west, seem to provide almost natural, though rough, constituency boundaries. The government has found, however, that the exact position of optimal constituency boundaries would be most difficult to establish without a comprehensive examination of all relevant factors. More importantly, it is

our belief that it is of the utmost importance to give the prime role in the determination of the boundaries to residents of the territories themselves and to provide a mechanism through which interested residents may present their views.
For this reason, the bill provides that this task be entrusted, under amendments to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, to an independent commission chaired by a judge and with two members to be chosen by the Speaker of the House from among the residents of the Northwest Territories. The representation commissioner would be the fourth member. The duty of this commission would be to consult with the residents of the Northwest Territories and to make recommendations for the setting of constituency boundaries with reference to ease of transportation and communication, to community of interest within constituencies and to maintaining a rough balance in geographical size between them. These factors have been selected as being of particular pertinence to the Northwest Territories.
In conclusion, I think we may be confident that the passage of this bill will, in conjunction with the Representation Act, ensure a distribution of seats in this House which not only will be just and equitable but also will provide Canada with a representative House equipped to face the challenges of the future.

Before I give some of the reasons why this is the case, may I make a suggestion to which the government House leader and my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) might give some thought. In light of the fact that the standing committee is seized with problems concerning other matters, in order to facilitate the passage of this bill I suggest some thought be given to considering it in committee of the whole and giving it third reading today. I offer the suggestion that on this interesting Friday afternoon we might deal in that way with this very important matter. We might speed its passage here and get it to the other place so that it may become law in ample time to carry out the studies to which the minister referred. I make this proposal on behalf of our party.
The Northwest Territories has always presented a very difficult problem with regard to representation. It has been fortunate, though, in getting good quality representation. I think back to the first member for the Northwest Territories, the late Merv Hardie, a friend of mine and of many people in this House. He was a good and effective member who did a great deal for the people of his constituency. Mr. Gene Rheaume, a member of this party, in the face of serious handicaps caused by the size of the constituency and other factors did a most effective job of representation in the opinion of most members of the House and, I believe, of his constituents.
February 28, 1975

The Northwest Territories needed people of this calibre because of its very nature, its vastness and extent. I have travelled through much of it. My hon. friend from Bran-don-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), a minister at one time, is familiar with the stresses which can result from the sheer size of this constituency which, in itself, is enough to cause a tremendous amount of anxiety in those who represent it. I notice that clause 7 of the bill refers to certain criteria which are to be borne in mind. It provides:
In preparing its report the commission for the Northwest Territories shall be governed by the following rules ... the commission shall give special consideration to the following factors:
(i)	ease of transportation and communications within the electoral districts;
(ii)	geographical size and shape of the electoral districts relative to one another; and
(iii)	any community or diversity of interests of the inhabitants of various regions of the Northwest Territories.
I come from a constituency to which those words could aptly be applied, as do many of my colleagues in this House. I recall that when the first bill dealing with the readjustment of boundaries was going through its various stages, words of that kind were used by myself in an attempt to persuade the commissions to make certain dispositions as to constituency boundaries. I am sure other members made the same point. It is comforting to know that at this stage the government has recognized that these are matters which have to be taken into consideration when drawing up electoral boundaries. I would hope that some time when we are reviewing the provisions of the general legislation, the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, criteria of this sort would be inserted because they constitute a very strong recommendation and one to which heed should be given by the commissions.
Representing, as I did, the old constituency of Peace River which occupied almost one third of the territorial mass of the province of Alberta, I can say that it presented, on a smaller scale, the same challenges in the way of representation as do the Northwest Territories, and these guidance rules would have been most useful.
We approve the legislation because we agree with what the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) has said. In addition, for too many years the affairs of the territories have been dominated by a form of neo-colonialism on the part of many of the officials of the department. I see signs, now, that this is disappearing but there is still a certain amount of it present. It constitutes a further problem for those who represent the constituency. I recall an old friend and colleague, the late Jack Sissons, the first judge of the territorial court of the Northwest Territories, engaging in a legal battle with the administration in an attempt to bring about an examination of a judicial matter of which he was fully seized so as to secure equity for the native people of the territories. One needs to read the autobiography of this distinguished jurist in order to understand how difficult it was for him, as it must have been for all the members from the Northwest Territories, to cope with this department. I am glad to see that some of the old attitudes are disappearing, and I think the process should be expedited. I believe the minister's intentions are good; the test will be his capacity to overcome the resistance which can still make itself felt in his department.
Northwest Territories
After long years of isolation because of conditions over which they had no control-I sometimes think they were fortunate-the native people of the territories have suddenly been faced with the impact of the twentieth century. In comparatively recent times the Northwest Territories have shown signs of yielding a number of valuable products which the outside world appears determined to discover, develop, process and send away to other parts of the country and the world. This has placed the Indian and Innuit people in immediate proximity to the benefits and also to the drawbacks of modern technology. They have not had an opportunity to prepare themselves over the years, and it has come as a tremendous shock.
Having spoken with the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), and from my own experience travelling there and talking to the people, I know precisely how difficult this transition has been for them. It will take a great many years before the difficulties of adjustment are successfully overcome. Conflicts of a social nature as well as of an economic nature have been emphasized to an extent unknown in other parts of Canada, and it has been exceedingly difficult for one member representing such a constituency to do the job that needs to be done.
Let me seize the opportunity on this occasion to suggest to the government that it expedite Bill C-3, which adds Senate representation for the Northwest Territories and Yukon, as soon as possible. These two bills are companion measures, and I am sure the government House leader will agree with me, especially if he can get the kind of co-operation that this party is offering from the party of my hon. friend to my left, that this course should be followed. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is just aching to urge that the distinguished body that is known as the other place should have among its membership a representative from the Northwest Territories.
For these reasons and a great many more that I could talk about for hours as a result of my knowledge of the needs in the north, we urge the House to give rapid passage to this bill at all stages and to send it to the other place.

I want to pay my particular respects to my colleague the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) for the persistence with which he has worked on this matter. As a member who has had to represent people spread over 1.5 million square miles, he is very much aware of how difficult it is for one person to represent that vast area and its far-flung population. He has felt that one of the best contributions he could make to his area and to his people is to insist that the Northwest Territories have two mem-

Northwest Territories
bers in the House of Commons, and we are delighted that his goal is being achieved.
I appreciate the reference made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) to the bills that the hon. member for Northwest Territories has placed before parliament, both in the twenty-ninth parliament and in this one. Bill C-299 is the hon. member's bill in this parliament and it calls for two seats for the Northwest Territories. The hon. member for Northwest Territories would like to compliment the government on finally having seen the wisdom of this proposal, and we are glad that this present bill, C-51, is to be put through all its remaining stages today.
I believe my colleague would agree with the suggestion made by the government-in fact, I know he agrees-that there be an independent commission to draw the line between the two seats. There are certain problems that must be looked at. In his bill my hon. friend suggested the names Mackenzie and Franklin for the two ridings. He tells me that since then he has been thinking about it some more, and that perhaps the logical names for the two ridings would be Western Arctic and Eastern Arctic. At any rate, this will be a matter to be decided by independent commission that will be appointed under the terms of the bill, after it hears from the people of the north, and we are glad that this action is being taken. We think this is an appropriate way to bring the people of the Northwest Territories, whose population is growing, as the minister pointed out this morning, into the mainstream of Canadian life, and we look forward to the fact that in the thirty-first parliament we shall have in this House of Commons two members from this area as well as a member from the Yukon.
I could have stopped here and resumed my seat, Mr. Speaker, but for the reference that the hon. member for Peace River dragged in at the end of his remarks. I have too much respect for the people of the north to palm off on them members who would be appointed by the government to sit in a house that is not elected by the people of Canada. Therefore, we shall give unanimous consent to this bill going to committee of the whole and to its being given third reading today, but don't ask us to deal today with Bill C-3. We want the north to be represented where the action is-here in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE REPRESENTATION AND ESTABLISH A COMMISSION TO READJUST ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some brief comments on this significant occasion. What is happening here today represents decades of effort toward achieving broader representation for the Northwest Territories. I think what is happening today would not have occurred had not the present member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) been elected. He is the first member from this great, vast geographic territory who is of native descent. I have long felt, both as a former minister of northern affairs and also as one interested in the development of the north before being appointed to that position, that the need for broader representation was recognized particularly by the native population.
My real purpose in participating in this debate today is to refer briefly to some of the historic facts that have emerged in the pursuit of more representative democracy in the north. It is only 22 years since the Department of

Northern Affairs and National Resources was established, with its first minister being the Hon. Jean Lesage. It was only in 1959 that the Indian population received the franchise, a very recent historical development. Only as recently as 1962 did the Eskimo population receive the right to vote in this country, a quite recent development.
I think tribute should be paid to a former prime minister of this country, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who is not with us today, because he more than anyone else can claim the credit for constantly keeping in view wider and more responsible representation for the north. It was under his administration that both groups of our native people received the right to vote for representation in the Parliament of Canada. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) long sponsored a bill providing for two members for the Northwest Territories as well as for the Yukon territory, and his name should be mentioned in passing this morning.
To deal specifically with the bill that is before us, it is actually going to accomplish what we attempted to accomplish in 1963. Those members of far off days who are still in the House will recall that a bill was before parliament at that time to divide the Northwest Territories into two territories-not two electoral districts but two territories. The idea was to achieve adequate representation from the eastern Arctic which is made up primarily of native peoples. The complaint had been heard repeatedly that it was impossible for the native people to receive adequate representation in the House of Commons because, in the first instance, they did not have the vote until 1962 and, in the second instance, they would be overwhelmed by the voting strength concentrated in other parts of the country.
As I said in my opening remarks, that problem has been overcome by the fact that we have representation in the House of Commons by a member of the native people. This is a tribute to the comparatively rapid development that has taken place on the basis of the great upsurge in education as well as in the economy. It is a tribute that this situation has come about within the short space of two decades since this parliament and the Government of Canada became specifically interested in the development of this 3.5 million square miles that make up the Northwest Territories.
One point I should like to make before concluding is that there is ample information available as a result of the consultations which took place in preparation for the division of the territories contemplated in the legislation before this House in 1963. Prior to the defeat of the Diefenbaker Conservative government, consultation had taken place over a long period of time. A lot of information was accumulated which would provide the helpful background information required as the government contemplates the establishment of two electoral districts in the Northwest Territories. In those days, consultation was the order of the day. When there was a change in government, the new government decided to establish a commission, namely, the Carrothers commission, which moved around the northern half of Canada and brought in recommendations that resulted in the disappearance of the idea to divide the territories into two areas.
February 28, 1975

Proposals have been made about naming the new constituencies, calling one Eastern Arctic and the other Western Arctic. I do not think that is good enough, in view of the romantic and historic past of the Northwest Territories. I would suggest that the name to be chosen for the new territory should be retained in the name of the electoral district. It is an Eskimo word-Innusiaq. I think it would be ideal for the purposes contemplated in Bill C-51.
There are many problems in the Northwest Territories but there has been tremendous progress as a result of policies introduced in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Now that, at long last, some dozen years after the proposition was first put before this House, we are achieving the kind of representation that has been urgently required, I hope we will be able to move forward in dealing with some of the problems well known to those in this chamber.
I again congratulate the hon. member for Northwest Territories on his initiative in this regard and trust that the bill will receive speedy passage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION AND PRESCRIBE REGULATIONS FOR LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize the importance of these proposals. The Farm Credit Corpora-
28996 -28'/2

February 28, 1975
Farm Credit Act
tion has administered this act for about 15 years and has made about 120,000 loans to farmers, totalling about $2 V* billion. That makes the Farm Credit Corporation the biggest single source of mortgage money for Canadian farmers, and it means that this piece of legislation is so important to Canadian farmers that it must be amended periodically to respond to the changing credit needs of the farm community. That is why these amendments are before the House today.
At the outset I must put in a plug for the pay-back record of farmers who have borrrowed under this program. In its 15 years of operation the Farm Credit Corporation has lost less than four cents on every $100 it has lent. I think this is something to brag about: we can brag about the honesty of the farmers who borrowed this money from the country, because they have been working under extreme conditions in order to pay back these loans. It also indicates that perhaps the Farm Credit Corporation was not taking the risks it should; just as the banking institutions do not take the risks that they should. Under the Bank Act they are allowed to charge interest rates that will cover a certain amount of risk, but if you ask them what they lose, the ratio is so small that you wonder if they are taking any risk at all. In this new Farm Credit Act we will be asking the Farm Credit Corporation to take more risks. I therefore ask the support of the House for the five major amendments which I propose.
The first amendment will increase the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation from $66 million to $100 million. This is important because the Farm Credit Corporation can borrow 25 times its capital from the federal Department of Finance. This, in effect, will allow the corporation to loan more money than in the past. This change is needed because farmers need more long-term capital today than ever before. Between 1951 and 1971, the total value of farm capital in Canada increased from $9.5 billion to $23.7 billion. The number of farms with annual sales of $5,000 has more than doubled. The number whose sales exceeded $10,000 increased by more than 500 per cent.
The second amendment is a technical one. Right now, the Farm Credit Act demands that the corporation take a first mortgage on land as security for loans. If this bill is passed, the Farm Credit Corporation could make loans on second or subsequent mortgages. It would give the farmers who already have a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation, or from some other loan organization, the option of getting a second and separate loan on a second mortgage. The first would not have to be renegotiated. A farmer who already has a first mortgage against his farm held by a lender other than the Farm Credit Corporation would also be able to borrow additional funds from the corporation on a second mortgage. If the first mortgage has a preferred interest rate, he would not have to change this. This would mean a saving to farmers who are lucky enough to have lower interest rates or better pay-back arrangements on their first mortgages than the Farm Credit Corporation could arrange if the two loans had to be consolidated as has been the case in the past.
Now we come to the most important part of the bill. There are three major amendments that will help young people to get started in farming. Look at the need. Between 1951 and 1971 the percentage of Canada's farmers

who were under 35 years of age dropped from 22 per cent to 15 per cent. This country cannot afford to let that trend continue. The demand for food will increase in our country and all over the world, so it is important for us to encourage more people to enter agriculture.
In recent years the Farm Credit Corporation has done a lot to tackle this problem. Between April 1, 1974, and December 31, 1974, 53 per cent of the corporation's loans were made to people under 35 years of age. We hope to make more than 5,000 loans to farmers under 35 years of age during 1975. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that according to letters received in my office and letters received by the Farm Credit Corporation and its district offices, many young people are waiting for this legislation to become effective.
Let us look at the three main features aimed at helping young farmers. Now, young farmers under the age of 35 who show above average management skills can get loans for up to 90 per cent of the productive value of their farm land and chattels. The amendments before the House call for even more, namely, for the making of loans of more than 90 per cent of the productive value of these assets to young farmers who have the drive and ability to make farming pay. In other words, we shall be lending money to young men according to their ability to farm, not according to how much money they have in the bank or in equity. That is the way most people think it should be.
We need this change because the market value of much of our best farm land has been forced to a much higher figure than its productive value. If we were to tie all our loans to the productive value of farm land, I am afraid this legislation would become worthless to many people wanting to buy a farm in the future. With the cost of land and chattels going up, it is also common sense to lift the maximum on our loans. This bill calls for maximum loan to farmers under 35 years to be increased to $150,000.
The bill also calls for a real breakthrough in our federal farm credit program. At present, loans can only be made to those whose main occupation is farming or will be farming once the loan has been made. That is no longer good enough. Many young men are able to get the backing they need to buy farm land, but need time before they can afford the livestock and equipment needed to make the farm generate enough income to cover both their farm bills and living costs. That is why we are proposing a new part to be added to the Farm Credit Act. Under it, we want to give loans to young people on condition that they become full-time farmers within five years. During this five-year period these young farmers will be able to hold regular jobs off the farm; this will help them get their farm operations under way.
As I have said, young farmers will be able to borrow as much as $150,000 under this legislation, plus an additional $50,000 under the Farm Improvement Loans Act for land, equipment, and so on. I think we should pass our stabilization legislation as quickly as possible so that both pieces of legislation can complement one another. If we lend money to young farmers, they must be assured that they will be able to pay back the money they have borrowed for land, equipment, and so on.
February 28, 1975

Some people in Canada have suggested that the state should own all the land. It would be terrible if that were to happen in Canada, if somebody decided that our farms should operate under such conditions. Our agricultural industry is the most productive industry in Canada; it has increased its productivity by 100 per cent per man in ten years, whereas the average industrial and commercial operation has Only increased its productivity by about 40 per cent per man in the last ten years. Our people deserve the right of private ownership. Most Canadians favour ownership of land. Most people who come to Canada from Britain, Europe and other parts of the world come here with the idea of owning land and being free to create something for themselves. To see that I am right all one has to do is examine conditions in countries where the state owns the land. Where the state owns it, there is not much incentive to produce: people are not prone to work so hard if they are not creating something for themselves; there is no incentive to work beyond a set time; there is no desire to run a combine all night if the weather for the next day is not promising. People on state-run farms prefer to stop in the middle of the afternoon. The same happens with the planting of crops. It is people who have pride of ownership, who want to create something, who are willing to work hard.

It is this, as I said earlier, which makes the 6 per cent of our people engaged in agricultural production our most efficient members of society. They have become so productive because there is the incentive to produce and create. Passage of this legislation, as well as of the stabilization legislation, is important if this momentum is to continue. Further, we can only guarantee the consumer that he will have a constant supply of high quality food at reasonable prices by passing legislation which will ensure a strong agricultural base in this country. The agricultural industry is extremely important for one third of our population in one way or another depends on it for jobs.
Any nation which does not have a healthy agricultural industry faces problems; its society is not healthy. So it is most important for us to pass this and other farm legislation as soon as possible. Our future food producers are the young farmers of today. They need this legislation which is important to all members of our society and I urge hon. members to give it to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has said in introducing this bill. He said this is one of the most important pieces of legislation on our statute books. I think most members of the House would concede that 20 years ago agriculture in all parts of Canada was in desperate straits. The government which assumed power in 1957 introduced a number of bills which still serve as guides for farm legislation: measures providing for stabilization of prices, for the Farm Credit Corporation, and so on, first introduced by the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) stand as landmarks for all western countries to behold. A social scientist who examined legislation in the western world listed farm programs which we introduced as the most revolutionary type of legislation passed by any
Farm Credit Act
country in the western world in the last 70 years. I am glad the minister recognizes this.
We must deal with agriculture on a non-partisan basis. Agriculture is our main force for solving the world's biggest problem, that of feeding the hungry people of the world. This will call for maximum effort in which our agricultural industry must play its part. That means it is our duty to work in a non-partisan way, in the interests of the people of Canada and of all the world, and make sure that agriculture is given the tools and the freedom to finish the job.
The minister's comments about the importance of young farmers deserve to be dealt with at length. I would like to add to the views expressed by the minister by saying that we have not begun, in the western world, to farm the way we will have to farm in the next 20 to 30 years. We have always had unlimited land to develop. We have become very expert in extensive agricultural techniques. By "extensive" I mean extending over large areas of land and farming them with the techniques we have learned in dry land farming. It has been a great evolution in the field of science to see areas of the world that were once considered desert, like Saskatchewan, become among the most productive areas of the world. This great evolution of moving into dry areas, mastering the difficulties there and producing food is one of the great wonders of the modern world, particularly in respect of the people who did it. However, it is not enough. We must turn, now, to techniques of intensive agriculture in order to multiply two and three times the quantities we produced before with the same amount of land, water and air. Young farmers will be essential in this task. I know something of their flexibility, staying power and willingness to take the chances that will be required and, above all, I know the willingness of farmers to work, because I know something of the difficulties that we face in this field.
I am glad the minister recognizes that you cannot deal with a single item like farm credit and think that is the answer to all the problems. It has to be related to other fundamental parts of the program. The first fundamental part is marketing. It is on this most important, first function of agricultural policy that this government is weakest and has been for many years. Second is the question of stability of prices. There will shortly be a bill dealing with this before the House. We look forward to it; it is a move in the right direction.
The third principle is stability of income. We have a bill before us this session which deals with that problem for western farmers but not for eastern farmers. The fourth principle is a modern system of farm credit. That is what we are discussing now. The fifth principle is redevelopment. That is another subject on which I will have a lot to say during the next few months, and on which I think this government is very weak. I ask the minister, with regard to redevelopment, to take back into his department the branches and divisions that have been stolen from agriculture and have downgraded the department over the past ten years. These five principles are the test for measuring gauge that we in this party will apply to all policies produced by the government. If they meet the test of forward motion, the official opposition will support them.

Farm Credit Act
With respect to these Farm Credit Act amendments, I support the legislation. I wish to point out that we in the Diefenbaker administration started this type of modern farm credit program in 1959. However, three years after we passed the legislation it was in need of reform because changes occurred so rapidly. I recall some of the reforms brought in under the regulations whereby farmers were allowed to pay a share of crop payments instead of a fixed interest payment and capital repayment. We discussed the need of Indians on and off reservations having access to this legislation. We discussed the problems of city people, ex-young farmers who found no opportunity on a group farm of several sons moving to the city and wanting to come back but not being able to do so because the legislation insisted that a man had to be a 100 per cent farmer to get any money.
All these things began to be apparent within a few years of our passing this legislation. The tragedy is that it has taken us so long to get to the stage where knowledge of the need has been translated into legislative proposals. In the life of a nation, ten years is not very long. However, in the life of a young person on the farm or in the city whose hopes and ambitions have been frustrated, ten lost years do not refer to the recession or the depression; they refer to how long parliament took to reform this farm credit legislation.
I recall the changes brought in by the minister who succeeded me. His proposal was that we should increase the maximums. However, it was he who broke the original pledge of the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert. In return for asking farmers who borrowed from the Farm Credit Corporation at 5 per cent interest when money could be borrowed at lower rates from other sources, we said if interest rates ever went above 5 per cent we would make sure that the farmers of this country could borrow at 5 per cent. It was an averaging or stabilizing device. The minister of agriculture who followed me broke the pledge and let interest rates rise. I will come back to that. Since that time we have had several amendments, mostly dealing with the size of loans, which have been of importance. However, today we have Bill C-34, before us. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we have several speakers on this side who will be making positive and, I hope, constructive proposals that will help improve this bill when we get it to committee.
My particular proposal deals with potential types of loans as opposed to loans on assets. I gathered from the minister's remarks that the criticisms of the Farm Credit Corporation in the past few years have dealt with the question of assets. We work like a group of bankers, on the assumption that before you lend any money you must have assets to equal the amount of the loan. Even though the proportion of assets is now down to 50 per cent or 60 per cent, I simply point out to the House-as I am sure thousands of farmers have pointed out to the government in the past ten years-that a young person, by no stretch of the imagination or in his wildest dreams, can ever accumulate the assets necessary for him to assume a huge loan.
What has actually happened is that the young man who wants to farm has had to ask his parents, uncles or neighbours to pledge their land in the taking out of a loan, even

though he is using the farm he is buying as one of the items of collateral. This means we have tied up the assets of the older generation who would like to move on to a little easier life after many years of hard work, but cannot get off their farming operations because their land is tied to backing a loan for a son or neighbour. The improvements in the bill really do not grapple with this problem. They do reduce the asset requirements and allow for second mortgages and other types of collateral. Instead of this, I ask the minister, who has always spoken up for agriculture, now to speak up loudly and clearly on this matter and say that he will see to it-he can do this without amending the act but through the regulations- that loans will be granted to young people without assets; that loans will be granted on the basis of a young man's ability to farm, to produce a good plan, to demonstrate that he knows how to succeed.
Is this idea so revolutionary? In 1934 the United States Congress during the Roosevelt period put such legislation on its books and it is still there. Any private lending agency in the United States is empowered to lend to any young farmer without assets the amount the lending agency feels fit for the type of operation contemplated. The only limitation placed on the application of that legislation is this: the young man has to bring in signatures of ten neighbouring farmers who know him and will vouch for his integrity and ability. They are supposed to put a nominal sum on the line as a guarantee of good faith when signing that document. I doubt whether in the last 25 years a United States bank or other financial agency has ever asked an individual to forfeit that deposit. When any young man can get ten farmers behind him, he is not very likely to fail: they do not do this to help a neighbouring lad unless they intend to ensure that he makes a success of what he is doing.
Here is another example. In the period between 1948 and 1959 the Ontario government had the young farmers loan act on its books, and even though the loans were not large they were granted mainly on the basis of the recommendation of neighbours of the applicant. I have not looked at that legislation for years, but my recollection is that in the 11 years of the operation, losses amounted to about $2,000. Millions of dollars were lent, yet there was only this minuscule loss. So these are not new ideas.
A third precedent was in 1958 when Canadian money was given to a foreign government, the government of Malaysia, for clearing the jungles for the farmers of that country as a means of preventing the infiltration of communists from the north. On selected ten-acre plots, bred rubber trees were planted on about seven acres and a variety of other plants on the remainder. Canadian money provided these Malaysian farmers with a monthly sum on which to keep their families alive until the rubber trees began to procedure seven years later. When these men obtained a cash flow equal to the cost of their farming operations, equal to the cost of looking after their families, the rest of their income was considered net income and the Canadian government asked for 15 per cent in return payment of the loan. That debt is now paid. Isn't it about time we did the same sort of thing for young Canadians?
February 28, 1975

I could go on to give other examples. However, I hope my proposal is acceptable to the minister. Let us see whether we can get away from all this red tape, tying up acreages all around the young people we are trying to help. Free the older generation to do as they like with their own farms. This is a matter which is on my conscience. I tried to make this change when I was minister of agriculture in 1962. I put it before the advisory committee of the Farm Credit Corporation on two occasions, but on both occasions it was turned down. I have regretted ever since that I did not use the power the people had given me to push it through: we could have had the legislation in place for the last 13 years. I urge the minister not to carry the load on his back that I have carried through my failure to get this help to our young people. I realize there have to be advisory committees. But they are only advisory committees; they are not our masters. The electors of this country are the people to whom we are responsible.
A similar thing happened to the minister of agriculture of Ontario. He proposed a scheme under which young farmers could go into the livestock business provided they stuck with it for seven years, at the end of which he would forgive them a large protion of the capital debt. His advisory board turned him down. I am saying to the minister, "Thirteen years ago I had my opportunity and I tried to push this proposal forward. I have carried this on my back for 13 years, and I hope you do not have to do the same thing."
It is about time we moved ahead in this field of loans and got away from the worshipping of assets. Other institutions, other interest groups have done so. The Bank of America, in California, developed its whole banking operations on the concept of lending money on the basis of cash flow, the earning power of the people to whom it was lending money. I would like to see this done for the young people in Canada who want to farm. If this was important 13 years ago when the average farm loan was around $10,000, it is even more important today when the average farm loan is around $45,000 with a ceiling of $150,000. It is not the amount of the loan which kills a borrower; it is the interest he has to pay because of high rates tied to the lending rate of the government with its inflationary ways of doing things. The effect is that over a 30-year period a young farmer will pay $3 in interest over and above the $1 he has borrowed; in other words, if he borrows $100,000 he knows he will have to pay $300,000 in addition by way of interest, under the present set-up.
I do not say farm productivity will not be able to afford this in the future, but it means that 75 per cent of a man's effort goes into payment of interest and only 25 per cent into repayment of money borrowed. The same thing applies to a person buying a home. The price of a home in Toronto now is $57,000. A person buying it will have to pay another $150,000 in interest. This is the logic of the capitalintensive economy in which we live.
I hope the minister is sincere when he tells us we have to support young farmers. I do not care whether the young man comes from a farm or from a city. With the tremendous emphasis today on knowledge of business techniques, some of our best farmers are coming from the cities. In the past we have discriminated against these people on the ground that they were city people, and very often they
Farm Credit Act
could get no help at all. This bill takes a big step forward. A young man may, if he wishes, continue to work in the city, but if it is understood that he intends to become a full-time farmer, money can still be lent to him. As I say, that is a big step forward. I hope we can tie it in with the proposal I have just made and remove this silly asset requirement. The asset requirement makes it impossible for nine out of ten young men to get a farm today; only one in ten has an uncle or a father on a farm.
Sitting in the gallery at the present time is a farmer with three sons who has already tied up his holdings to get two sons started. He has a third son now ready, but the farmer is still young and he wants to keep on farming. At the same time he is helping a neighbour lad. I know he is a young farmer because he is the same age as I am, but he has three sons and a neighbour boy who are ready. All his assets are tied up for all the years the sons will take to pay off the debts. So I plead not only for the sons but for the old man too.
Secondly, I suggest that besides the concept of potential lending, which has a record of little or no losses, we should look for a new method of payment. My second proposal is that if a farmer comes into a plan, particularly a livestock plan which means a five-year to seven-year pay-out period before he can get going, during that period we should not take any repayments from him. Then when he does get a cash flow, the first charge on that cash flow should be the cost of operation and an agreed amount for his living. The balance will be considered net.
I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and those gnomes who advise him will argue very strenuously against this type of proposal, but I also know that it is actuarially sound. If you allowed the farmer his cost of operation and family living, the government would get more money back at a faster rate if it took 15 per cent of the net rather than a 6 per cent interest rate. With a loan level of 8 per cent, perhaps it would have to be split 18, 19 or 20 per cent to the 82 to 80 per cent to get your money back; but there would be peace of mind for the young man who borrowed this huge sum of money. He would have the knowledge that his family would be looked after, that his operation operating cost would be looked after, and when he gets a cash flow he would not object to paying 15 to 18 per cent of his profit to the Farm Credit Corporation which lent him the money. This figure would have to be projected on a percentage basis, a calculation the Farm Credit Corporation is well qualified to make.
This new type of repayment proposal would mean that during a period of two or three bad years, such as the livestock producers are now experiencing, they would not lose their shirts or their farms. When crops and returns are exceptionally good, as they were two or three years ago in the livestock industry, a return of 15 to 18 per cent of the net to the government would be much greater than it would with a 6 to 7 per cent interest rate. As I say, this has been done in Malaysia and it can be done here. It would be up to the minister to fight it out with the Department of Finance to see whether it could be done.
We are talking here, admittedly, about young people. How many will there be? I have looked over the tables but

Farm Credit Act
I do not think the number of young people demanding these loans at the beginning will be more than 2,000 or 3,000, with perhaps an additional 1,000 a year from then on in, though I may be wrong about that. I suggest the Minister of Finance would be better off to take 15 per cent or 18 per cent of the net profit, though the exact percentage would of course have to be agreed upon. I would particularly recommend this proposal for those who come off reservations or farm on Indian reservations. In my district a farmer and his associates saved for ten years while on an Indian reservation. Finally they saved $10,000 and in 1974 received a very large loan; Indian Affairs was very generous to them. However, the interest rate and a fixed rate of return in the livestock business could break this man's and his wife's heart over the next two or three years. There are five or six other families on the same reservation fighting now to save a few dollars and their life's dream could also be destroyed. What I am describing in my own constituency I am sure could be described by other members with Indians in their areas.
I think the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), with all the willingness in his department to help if they only knew how, would be sympathetic to some kind of repayment scheme based on a share of the profit. I ask them not to worry about incentive. If you give a guy 80 to 85 per cent of the profit, he will work. I suggest these proposals are worthy of consideration and I hope they will be matched by other proposals from our side of the House. I conclude my remarks by saying that Bill C-34 is a good bill. The amendments in it are good amendments. All I ask is that in the committee the minister sit down on a non-partisan basis and try to make it a heck of a lot better.
