speechtext:
Stanley and I are united on this point. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, we can deal with this bill very quickly. We support the amendments, particularly those relating to additional loans that are now being made to young people. They are worth while and they are, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said, long overdue. A debate like this gives us an opportunity to stress once again to all members of the House, particularly those from rural Canada, that we have an obligation to say to those from urban Canada that it is very important to build a strong agricultural industry; particularly in a country such as ours where agriculture is the economic base.
Canada is one of the few countries of the world that produces a surplus of food, and it should be our moral obligation to produce as much food as we can. This is our obligation to mankind, particularly at a time when so

many people in the world are dying from lack of food. We see expanding populations in all nations of the world and diminishing agricultural producing areas due to the madness with which mankind plans cities today by putting concrete over good agricultural land and topsoil. Thus, this country and the parliamentarians in this House are obligated to make the number one priority in this country the maximization of food production, not only for the people of Canada but for all mankind.
I urge upon the government that the only way it can do this is by providing farmers with a stable economy and price guarantees so they will know in the spring what they are going to get in the fall. The farmer, like anyone else in our society, is faced with many things he cannot determine. He is faced, first of all, with world climatic conditions; he cannot determine rainfalls and he cannot determine frosts; he cannot determine what conditions will be in China, the Soviet Union or elsewhere. He cannot control international markets. Because of these uncertain and unknown factors, the farmer needs from the Government of Canada and the provincial governments as many guarantees as they can possibly muster. These guarantees must be of the following order. There must be, first, a price guarantee for his produce. That is a basic necessity. Second, and this is where I disagree with members of the Conservative Party particularly, there must be very strong marketing boards so the farmer has some clout in the marketplace. The marketing board should be for the farmer what the trade union is for the worker, what the professional association is for the lawyer and the doctor, what the real estate association is for the real estate agent, and so on. The farmer needs that type of clout in the marketplace and he needs that type of vehicle to enable him to bargain for the best justifiable future. He does not have that advantage in the market structure of today.
If the farmer is guaranteed those things, he will produce food. If he produces all the food possible, Canada can make a real contribution for the hungry people of the world. In the past we have been faced with the disgrace of food surpluses in this country. It was scandalous a few years ago when the government paid farmers not to grow wheat. I think most members of this House now realize that was a mistake. Instead of putting money into growing wheat, the funds should have been put into storage facilities in this country and into developing programs to help farmers diversify into other areas of food production. I think it was a tremendous mistake to pay farmers not to grow wheat.
Last fall we experienced another surplus. That was the CEMA surplus of eggs which resulted in great controversy. We would not have had a surplus of eggs in this country if there had been proper storage facilities and a proper delivery system in order to channel the eggs to countries where they were needed. We could have powdered and processed those eggs for storage and provided them as part of our foreign aid program to countries which needed them. We can use all the surpluses of food we can produce in this country, through foreign aid, by establishing a world food bank, a Canadian food bank or what have you, and feeding the starving people of the world. That should be our number one priority. When it comes to food
February 28, 1975

production, we must maximize that production in this country for the sake not just of the agricultural economy but for all people in the world.
The bill before us contains a number of important amendments which, as I have said, all of us are willing to support and endorse wholeheartedly. We in this party have been suggesting for years that we should make credit available at lower interest rates, easier terms and fewer restrictions for our young farmers. If one looks around the farming economies, including my own riding, he will find that the farmers' average age is 57. What does that say about farming today? I am sure the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and members from other cities in this country realize that when the average age of the workers is in the area of 57, something must be wrong with industry, in terms of planning.
If this trend continues in agriculture, for instance, we will have fewer farms and farmers. If that happens, we will have fewer small, rural communities, towns and villages and it will destroy the whole fabric of this lifestyle. That destruction will occur even if there is affluence in some farming areas because of the high price of wheat, but when that happens there will be an economic change. What will happen then is that the large farms will become larger because the owners or the farm corporations will buy out the small farms, put in bigger equipment and machinery and continue to expand their operations. That will continue unless we adopt programs which take chances on young farmers, giving them more money- hopefully, interest free. We must give them all the encouragement we can in order that they can firmly establish themselves in the farm business.
If I can get the minister's ear for one minute, I should like to tell him that the one thing he should be very concerned about is trying to get the Farm Credit Corporation and other branches of his department working in that way to improve the situation in practical terms. The land bank development program and the storage program in Saskatchewan are good examples of this. We must maximize co-operation between the provincial governments and the federal government. These programs in Saskatchewan are working very well, but they would work even better if we had more co-operation from Ottawa. I think the people of Saskatchewan will endorse these programs pretty heavily this June or July, whenever the election is held in that province, and I believe the minister is very much aware of that.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and the Minister of Agriculture referred earlier to the great contributions the various parties have made to agriculture and the farming economy. I think it goes without saying that this party has always been concerned about the welfare of the farmer. In fact this party was, basically, born among the farmers and the urban workers on the prairies. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), the late Mr. Coldwell and others of our party have represented farming constituencies and were elected basically because the farmers of this country wanted a change and a new political regime. They wanted some clout in the marketplace, some bargaining power. Our party fully realizes that if we are to have a sound national economy we must fulfil our obligations in respect
Farm Credit Act
of world humanitarian values, and the farming economy is where we must start.
I hope this bill passes second reading today, is moved expeditiously through committee and third reading stages and becomes law as quickly as possible so that the farmers of this country can enjoy the benefits of these amendments.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATION AND PRESCRIBE REGULATIONS FOR LOANS
speechtext:
After the statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) referring to possible improvements in farm credit, I realize this is needed in the present system and I shall certainly support the legislation, which is capable of improving the farmer's state of affairs.
He mentioned our young farmers, and I commend him for that. I also appreciated his reference to collective farming in certain European countries and all the drawbacks involved in such a system. He gets there my wholehearted approval. However, I should be very much pleased if we could have here in Canada a system where farmers would get some return from their farming operation without having to go into debt all the time. That is the current situation.
I realize that under present conditions loans are needed because the system is inherently stupid. But nonetheless, farming, as any other operation, should be organized in such a way that the operator could get his living out of it. How come it was found some 40 years ago that families of 12 children could live on the land but nowadays they cannot make ends meet with reduced families? All the problems they have come from somewhere. I find amazing we do not stop long enough to analyze that situation.
Credit is vital to many of our good operators, and even more so to the average farmer. I will give an example of how the Farm Credit Corporation's attitude can influence rural development in one area. One appraising criterium that biases the whole long term credit philosophy is the market value. The Farm Credit Corporation and the Farm Credit Board are similar agencies. Being in essence the only lenders, it may be concluded that they determine the market value of farms. If they do not lend, or not enough, clearly the selling price will be directly influenced by the amounts made available to borrowers. We are in a vicious circle. The officials will cynically say at times: "There is no buyer." Indeed, they are the only buyers, because no other business can compete with a Crown corporation funded with public grants. I wonder sometimes whether for the sake of profit we are not altering the objectives sought by the sponsors of this bill. Are the welfare measures which are mostly financed by the federal government not used to counterbalance the irresponsibility of some departments, such as the Department of Agriculture, and more specifically the Farm Credit Corporation?
When will the various branches of the federal government and the Crown corporations consider themselves as part of a single enterprise serving all Canadian citizens? Then, those mighty brains who work in complete isolation like independent private concerns and insist above all on profitability and efficiency would make the federal

February 28, 1975
Farm Credit Act
administrative machinery more profitable and efficient, and especially more acceptable to all Canadians.
Since now we see how rural life can avoid the miseries of urban life, the on-going crises between capital and work, the moral downfall of the capitalistic economy, we are still reluctant to grant the farming community full social and economic equality and allow them to organize their own environment and institutions.
Consequently, since the industrial organization of agriculture inevitably results in the disappearance of thousands of family farming operations at a time we should be filling the country with free and happy people, Montreal residents come down to settle in Kamouraska. Five families left the city to settle in Kamouraska in a rural environment. If I took a little time to relate the history of Kamouraska you would see that for a little over 50 years certain facts have been reminding us of circumstances which surrounded the establishment of the experimental farm in Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. I could quote debates in this House relating that the then federal member for Kamouraska participated in the establishment of the experimental farm in Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. Those are facts and, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, what is sad about all that is that farmers contributed to enlarging rural areas. I am talking about Kamouraska but that is also taking place in the whole province of Quebec, at least in the areas I had an opportunity to visit in Canada. Farmers managed 50 years ago with quite ordinary means to raise their families on lands of 100 acres or even sometimes 30 acres. Today those same families can no longer live without sinking deeply into debt. We must expand, we need pools to borrow, to organize the whole farming apparatus because very expensive machinery is required.
I am not against evolution, I take part in it, at least I try, and I keep up with the times. I try to follow the current evolution. But we must face facts as they are, considering the situation.
At this point in time, we should be populating our rural areas with free and happy citizens, to cultivate the soil instead of exploiting it, because there is a difference between the two. We should be taking care of the small and average units, according to their strength and the requirements of modern work and play. Instead, we are advocating solutions adapted to the industrial world, that is, increasingly cumbersome operations, which are economically delicate and humanly crushing.
Could it be that simply to decrease the democratic freedom and strength, the first for money and comfort of a class of society far too long deprived of them is being exploited? But what will be the ultimate results of such a policy on rural citizens and society as a whole?
One cannot go into debt indefinitely. It is unthinkable that a just society should stem from general indebtedness. To my mind, that is just common sense.
At a time when agriculture as a whole seems terribly complicated, where the answers given by the technocrats and politicians to rural problems seem increasingly remote from the needs and aspirations of a growing part of the population, might it not be advisable to come back to the basic principles of the social order our institutions strive 
to maintain, if only in an attempt to see whether the changes brought about through "a shower of laws" may not be contrary to the philosophy that has guided the organization of our rural society?
A society cannot be changed overnight. As any living organism, it can adapt itself to new conditions but gradually. To go too fast would threaten the organism with destruction from stress. In politics, contrary to what happens in the biological world, antibiotics cannot be used to cure ills quickly. That is why the passing of legislation must be approached with caution.
Social order is the result of thousands of painful situations experienced by mankind. Through the ages man clung to a certain number of principles. They enabled him to survive, guide his actions and bequeath a moral code to his descendants.
Today as yesterday, bread, science and religion are the three sources of human wisdom. Little by little man came to see himself as sociable, that is dependent upon others to fulfill his needs from birth to death. He thought necessary and best for him that individuals formed groups and took the responsibility of meeting various needs. Social classes defined themselves more or less successfully, with more or less control over the political power having become ever more necessary.
In this great scheme, farmers have always been the losers, in spite of the important part they were playing. As providers of physical necessities, isolated in their fields, farmers had to stay away from the market place where social and political deals are made and where the complex relations within the governing classes are established.
I remember the good old days of my youth in Kamouraska. We had politicians who apparently were high quality speakers. There is a sentence, among others, which still sounds fresh in my memory. A speaker was trying to win voters over to his side during a political meeting. Because these voters were farmers, he had chosen his words accordingly. Here is this sentence: "What profession is as noble as that of the farmer who, in the shadow of the parochial church steeple, ploughes a straight furrow to feed his family and mankind as well."
Such were the sentences used by Grit or Tory politicians in Kamouraska over 40 or 50 years ago. The man who uttered it was elected and was eventually appointed minister. Later, they came to realize the adverse effects of the current system: a whole population in debt. Try and prove me wrong!
The farming community shouldered more than its share of the nonsense of privileged classes, by letting them do sometimes the greatest stupidities. That is probably why the tyrants, who were aware of the farmers' restrained patience, have always attempted to maintain them in slavery. Without the latter's docility, the laziness and social vices of the groups in power would have not been possible. Let us mention incidentally that things have hardly changed, but for the refinement of methods and language to achieve the same purposes.
It is worth noting that farmers have never been able to get from society the proper price for their work. It is true. Let us just look at the current fight in all provinces in an
February 28, 1975

attempt to establish a reasonable price, a reasonable salary for the land worker.
A society can be considered free when its citizens can assume by themselves the responsibilities deriving from their lives, the lives of their families, from their paying taxes, and we know there are lots of those! They must assume the cost of the institutions necessary for the maintenance of their culture, their own social and economic progress, but without deeply sinking into debt.
One only has to look at what is going on to see a true reflection of our society: deserted farms, migration to the cities, which do not always give people the security they wanted.
One need not be surprised then that such a society finds it difficult to provide sound legislation made for free people but only offers to farmers as well as to other citizens the limitations of its industry and the instability of its liberal economy.
More serious still, it no longer provides farmers with the instrument of corporations, which encouraged responsibility and initiative, but with unions which can unfortunately be dominated and put to silence more easily because they invariably challenge an order they did not contribute to build.
We remember what happened last fall. I have here copies of newspaper clippings showing farmers killing animals and hanging them along the national highway. I say this myself. Cattle was killed by the hundred! They somehow repeated here what was done in the United States. Is this a normal situation? People complain, and it is true that a part of mankind is starving, and here we bury hundreds of animals, fattened calves that are ready for the market and that are destroyed. This happens here in Canada, in our system based on debt, which people do not want to change. We are going to suffer the consequences of that system, because it can certainly not bring about a just society. Again, we cannot found a just society on debt.
In the present circumstances, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, and with such a stupid system, we have to try to find the means to allow the farmers, the young people who want to go into farming-and I know there are some-to get the money required to purchase a property, develop it, put it in debt if they want. Everyone is in debt in our upside down system. This is not the answer.
In such a stupid system, we sometimes have to support legislation which can bring a bit of help and some temporary relief. This is not the answer. Can anyone think: My problem is solved because I am in debt. Come on! When you are in trouble and that a loan comes in handy, it might prove helpful, but does it solve the problem?
I shall conclude my remarks since I believe that I have said all that I wanted to say this afternoon about this bill. In passing, I would like to tell the minister that he can make all the necessary amendments to the bill to improve it, and particularly to avoid this famous bureaucracy and red tape. He should improve the bill so that the farmer who needs a loan may obtain it and so that the young man who wants to get into farming does not have to wait for months and go through a lot of red tape. Now, you have to wait indefinitely before obtaining a loan.
Farm Credit Act
I would like the procedures to be more flexible and I would like this bill, that I will support even though I am against running into debt, to be flexible enough to benefit the greatest possible number of Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure, and with hope for the future of young farmers and of agriculture that I rise to take part in this debate. I can certainly give my whole-hearted support to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who has presented this bill, to amend the Farm Credit Act, in order that long term mortgage credit may be made available to farmers, particularly young farmers. It is important that young people be given the opportunity to enter agriculture, and indeed we must try to divert some from other fields of endeavour that they may have chosen as their life's work.
Many pages have been written in the press, and the volumes of Hansard have recorded the words spoken in this House about the outstanding ability of the Minister of Agriculture-

Of course there have been some words to the contrary, but they have been shown to be weak and insipid when tested against the measures brought forward by the minister and put into practice by the government. Politics aside, Mr. Speaker, I firmly believe that a man's true worth is explained and upheld by his accomplishments. If the minister continues to bring in legislation such as the bill before us today and the Farm Stabilization Act, which attempt to rectify serious problems in agriculture, then the future of that industry and the future of this country are in good hands.
We must realize, Mr. Speaker, that the future of this country depends on the stability of the people engaged in agriculture. We can make all manner of brave and gallant statements about petroleum requirements and the problems of people in that industry, of the people who build our cars and who run our trains but, when it comes down to it, unless we have a stable agricultural industry all else is meaningless.
People in this country and indeed throughout the world can do without many things now regarded as necessities. We do not all need an automobile or two television sets- but we all have to eat. I think the best thing that we, as a nation, can do to help world conditions is to ensure that our agricultural industry remains stable. It is an industry which should be capable of meeting the food requirements of the world population.
People have talked about what causes wars. We have seen wars, develop in the past. Basically, wars have been brought on because nations have been unable to feed their

February 28, 1975
Farm Credit Act
people. If we are to play an auspicious part in preventing war and hate between nation and nation, we must look to the future and encourage our young people to take up the business of agriculture. Let us remember that, no matter what we say or do, agriculture is the backbone of our national foundation.
We can get along without many so-called amenities, but we cannot get along without our young people, who are basic to our well-being. Members representing the rural ridings, whether in the east or the west, in British Columbia or the Maritimes, know that young people are leaving the land and going to the cities, often for education. I know this holds true in the ridings of Perth-Wilmot, Huron, Dufferin-Grey-Simcoe-Waterloo, and many others; young people are leaving the ridings and seeking an education in the cities. We must reverse the present trend. We must induce these young people, once they have obtained the education they so richly deserve, to return to the land and take up food production.
This bill represents an important step forward in encouraging young people to take up the production of food, for the benefit not only of this country but of all the world. I have talked to the Minister of Agriculture about this bill, and I believe him when he says that this is one of the best pieces of legislation he has ever presented to this House because it will enable him to induce young people to take up farming. The minister can say to them, "Your country needs you as farmers. You can provide a service which will be of benefit to your country and to the world. This legislation, together with the farm stabilization bill, will assure you of a place in our country's future."
An hon. member participating in this debate said that the average age of farmers in his constituency is 57 years. In some constituencies the average age is even higher. We are fast approaching the time when many of our farmers will want to retire, as they deserve to do. They have worked long and hard. Our farmers are unlike any other people because they do not work by the clock; they do not even work by the sun. They work as long as necessary, doing what must be done in fields and barns. We can now say, "You have the right to retire because young people will enter farming." They can take up the business of agriculture without dragging their fathers, grandfathers and uncles into debt with them. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) touched on this point.
That part of the bill which will allow prospective farmers to work in the labour force for five years and then take up full-time farming is especially deserving of praise.
Most members of this House come from some type of farm background, even though many of them do not represent rural ridings. Many come from a stable, farm-oriented background, including the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis), and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) who comes from my area of the country, and is one of our most honoured citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) visited my riding some weeks ago he spoke of this legislation and hoped the opposition would not delay its passage. I have waited for it patiently and am glad that we can debate it today. The people of my riding enjoyed his visit, as did I.
As I have been personally involved in a farm operation, I can say with truth that farming requires management skills and capital. But, as well, many unknowns and variables enter into agriculture, and young farmers must be willing to allow for these variables. Fortunately the Farm Credit Corporation legislation provides for flexibility. This is necessary, as farm input costs are increasing rapidly.
People often comment on western farmers receiving, as they say, a bonanza of hundreds of millions of dollars for sales. That money is not really a bonanza, as the farmer has to pay ever increasing costs in order to grow his crops. Every farmer knows this is so.
Remember, as well, that when a young man takes up farming he must often live in an isolated area of the country where he will not have access to recreational amenities such as are available to people living in urban areas.
All these things are faced by a young man as he ponders going to the Farm Credit Corporation to get a loan. This is why I believe the government has to provide some incentives to young farmers getting into agriculture, in the same way it is providing incentives to industry. It is only right for the government to increase the limits for young farmers. However, it must also be concerned about the ability of the farmer to repay a loan.
I support the proposals put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). One proposal was to allow a young farmer to back his loan on the basis of the potential production of his land. He could
February 28, 1975	COMMONS DEBATES	3683
defer payment in a bad year and make a payment in a bumper crop year. It is important that a young farmer getting into agriculture should know that in a bad year he will not lose his farm and the amount of work he put into it.
Young people getting into agriculture today are burdened by debt. The initial financial outlay for land and machinery is increasing rapidly. The Farm Credit Corporation must realize that land around urban areas is generally the best agricultural land in Canada. However, because of the real estate value of the land the cost is escalating at a very rapid rate.
The Farm Credit Corporation allows loans on the assessed or appraised value of the land. However, that is not adequate. There are many examples of this in my riding. The assessed or appraised value of the land might be as low as $2,000 or $3,000 per quarter, but the land is selling in the real estate market for as high as $20,000 a quarter.
In and around the city of Edmonton the appraised value of agricultural land is $35,000, but the real estate value is upwards of $100,000. The land is productive. That is why I feel that the corporation must look at the potential productive value of the land. If 70 bushels of barley per acre have been grown for a number of years, that should be the base on which loans are made. It is not adequate to operate on the appraised value of the land.
Many young farmers come to me as their member of parliament. They complain that once the Farm Credit Corporation looks at what they propose to pay for land, it says it is too high and turns down any loans. If the loans were made on the potential productive value of the land it would be more fair and reasonable for young farmers trying to get into agriculture.
Some weeks ago I presented a private member's motion. I am sure the minister is familiar with it. I made four proposals. I do not intend to go into them in detail now. One proposal was with regard to deferred interest payments during the initial period. This is important to a young man going into agriculture. If in the first two, three or even five years he can pay back a certain amount of his principal without any interest, it will be reduced dramatically. He could then pick up the deferred amount of interest.
In the first few years a young farmer requires a substantial capital outlay. He may not have assessed all the input costs that come forward in the first few years of farming. If his interest were deferred he could put his profits toward the principal, and after a number of years start paying the interest. That would be a great incentive to a young man looking at such a large outlay of capital.
The minister is proposing that the amount of a loan to a farmer be increased to $150,000. In many cases this may be adequate. However, many people in agriculture today look at it as an industry. In many cases an economically viable unit costs more than $150,000. I will give an example.
A farmer and his two sons in my constituency are prepared to go into a dairy operation. The operation, including cattle, barns, silos and land, will cost somewhere around $400,000. However, Farm Credit will only allow them the maximum $150,000 because, no matter how many
Farm Credit Act
people want to operate that farm, it is still considered as a single unit. In situation like this the minister should allow each man to borrow the maximum. In this case, which involves three men, they should each be permitted to borrow the maximum $150,000. This would permit them to have an economically viable unit which would provide an income for all three. They would not have to go to other lending institutions which often charge higher interest rates than the Farm Credit Corporation.
I wish to make another positive proposal with regard to Farm Credit. The provinces have been filling the gap where Farm Credit leaves off. If a young man is outside the regulations of the Carm Credit Corporation, he has no alternative but to go to the province and make a loan from the Agricultural Development Corporation, or something similar. What is good about the provincial farm programs is that they have set up appeal boards. These boards are made up of local farmers and can consider each case individually.
The Farm Credit Corporation should take a long, hard look at setting up what I would call zone appeal boards. Respected farmers who have long established farms could sit on the regional board which would consider young farmers on the basis of their potential. They would have the final say as to whether a man would be approved for farm credit. This has worked well in a number of provinces. Perhaps the Farm Credit Corporation could work in conjunction with the provincial schemes.
Another proposal often put forward by members on this side is that a farmer who has attended college and meets some requirements, such as increased efficiency or increased yield, should be given a reduction in interest for principal. It would be an incentive to young men entering agriculture to attend Manpower courses in order to increase their management ability and efficiency.
It is also necessary to open-end mortgages. Many farmers going into agriculture for the first time have to start with a small basic unit. As they progress they find it is in their best interest to increase the amount of land or livestock on their farm. However, because Farm Credit is a closed mortgage, they have to pay lawyers' fees and again go through all the red tape that was necessary for the first mortgage. Therefore, open-end mortgages would be a saving for farmers.
Another proposal is the setting of a definite maximum interest rate, as proposed by my hon. friend from Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain, so that when a farmer looks at his loan he will know the interest rate will be a maximum of 6 or 7 per cent; it will never rise above that figure and he will never have to pay more, because if the interest rate goes down he would only be called upon to pay the lower rate.
We should take a hard look at these proposals in committee. In closing, may I say I believe this to be a good bill, one for which we have been waiting for a long time. I hope we can make it a still better one.

speechtext:
I, too, join with my colleagues in welcoming this particular piece of legislation. It is something we have been hoping for all during

February 28, 1975
Farm Credit Act
the twenty-ninth Parliament and through the thirtieth Parliament.
I do want to express one very real concern to the minister. It is my opinion that the legislation may be too late for this crop year. I do not wish to be pessimistic, but it appears to me, in practical terms, that by the time the legislation is in place it is doubtful it will have the impact I know the minister wants it to have, or indeed the impact those of us who are speaking to the bill want it to have in the 1975 crop year.
I know the minister is anxious to have the legislation proceed through the House as expeditiously as possible and passed on to the committee. But I know, too, Madam Speaker, that it is unreasonable to expect this. Having waited in excess of two and a half years for this particular legislation, and having sat all through the twenty-ninth Parliament with only one agricultural bill before us, we sympathize with the minister over the fact that agricultural policies are on the bottom rung of the priority list of the cabinet. We will do everything we can to assist the minister to improve that priority.
It would be interesting to attempt to deal with some of the detail of the bill, but I simply suggest to the minister that second reading is not the time at which to do it. I hope that in committee we will be prepared to discuss not just the technical aspects of the bill but such things as legal fees, a problem Farm Credit has ignored for far too long, open-end mortgaging, as has just been mentioned, refinancing, the regulations and guidelines Farm Credit representatives are operating under, valuation, and so on.
With respect to the maximum amounts of $100,000 and $150,000 as the case may be, I was interested to see in the last report of the Farm Credit Corporation that while the size of the average loan had increased substantially in the last fiscal year, we were still operating with average loans of less than $45,000. I have to ask myself, as I am sure the minister does, whether farmers want a loan of the maximum amount in the face of the intolerable burden of interest.
In other words, will more benefit be given to the larger farmer while the smaller farmer is continually facing more discouragement? This has certainly been the situation with respect to some farm policies, and indeed some Farm Credit policies. I hope that the minister and those of us in committee will have a long, hard look at this aspect because it seems to me that a large farm operation can take greater advantage of the maximum loans by spreading the burden over a much wider operation than its neighbour who is operating a small family farm.
The particular point I wish to make with some emphasis-and I will try to be as brief as possible-has to do with the price of land which has been mentioned in the report of last year from the Farm Credit Corporation. The president pointed out that farm land prices rose more in the year ending June, 1973, than they had in any previous year since records were kept, starting in 1910. He pointed out that in that year ended June 1973, farm prices had increased 17 per cent compared to an increase of 2 per cent in the previous year. The increases ranged from 21 per cent for Ontario to 13 per cent for Alberta.
| Mr. Jarvis. |
I don't think it takes any kind of a genius to see why they rose. Larger farms were obviously getting bigger which increased the demand for agricultural land. There was another very disturbing demand for land for nonagricultural use by the non-agricultural buyer-the pressures on city dwellers were such as to encourage them to move into rural areas. There was the obvious demand by land speculators. Then again, I think likely the largest demand with which we have to come to grips is the purchase of farm land by individuals who are not speculating but merely investing as the best possible hedge against inflation.
Finally, increasing the demand for agricultural land have been the actions of government itself. I think that all of us realize that Pickering is a prime example because so many farmers from the Pickering area-good farmers- have moved into my area and I am sure into the area of the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Douglas), where they have bought land at prices which, in the opinion of our farmers, were simply not competitive. They have been able to do so because the Pickering farmers had the funds with which to purchase the land at those inflated prices. While I am reluctant, indeed almost afraid to quote Mrs. Plumptre to the minister, I thought the statement she made about the loss of farmland at Pickering was one which the minister and I could both regard with sympathy.
With respect to the supply of land I would also point out to the minister that according to some experts-and I have heard all kinds of figures as I am sure he has-we are losing the prime land of southwestern Ontario due to the expansion of urban areas at the rate of 28 acres per hour.
I simply have to ask myself and the minister: what will this bill do? In isolation it is a good bill. In terms of farm credit it is a good bill. But in the larger context of land use and total farm quantity I have some very serious reservations. There are those who say to me, and I am sure they have said the same thing to the minister, that higher ceilings on Farm Credit Corporation mortgages are in themselves inflationary in their effect on farm land prices. I do not think these statements come from irresponsible people or from people who have not studied the problem. If we increase the limit of a Farm Credit loan I think we should ask ourselves very seriously: is this, in itself, likely to be a factor in increasing the price per acre of our farm areas, particularly in southwestern Ontario? I am sorry I cannot suggest to the minister what the answer to these questions is, but in the larger context of the farm economy that it is something with which we have to come to grips.
I was very impressed, I believe it was in the twenty-ninth Parliament, to see either in the Speech from the Throne or in the budget speech, a whole paragraph devoted to the government's concern regarding land use. It went on to say that there must be consultation with the provinces. What disturbs me, is that since that time we have not heard one word about that particular problem in the federal context, and I do not think that we can solve a problem simply by increasing farm credit limits when we have that tremendous albatross of increased demand, lower supply and speculation around our necks. Until we get to grips with the larger problem the minister will be coming back to this House repeatedly with bills such as this simply to catch up with events.

If we continue with 17 per cent as the rate of inflation in farm and prices annually, the minister will have to come back almost annually to give us higher limits. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the few minutes remaining to us I should like to discuss one or two points with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation. At the outset I would say that Bill C-34 has my entire support. I welcome the fact that it is before us today. I should like to see it become law and be proclaimed at an early date.
I should like to mention the need for capitalization, about which a number of members have spoken today, as well as the need for risk capital for young farmers. I should like to relate my remarks here to a specific problem in Manitoba. I echo the words of the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) when I say it is my view that even more money should be placed in the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation for loans to young farmers. I say that for this reason. In Manitoba in the last month we have run into serious difficulty as a result of the operations of the Manitoba Agricultural Credit Corporation. As has been mentioned, a number of provinces have set up provincial agricultural corporations, not necessarily to supplement but to increase the amount of money available to farmers for farming purposes.
What is happening in Manitoba now is that farmers are reacting by asking me whether it would be possible to increase the amount of money available from the Farm Credit Corporation, not only through Bill C-34 on an individual basis, but the total amount of money made available. These farmers are not able to get sufficient money, and so are forced to apply for a loan to the Manitoba Agricultural Credit Corporation.
Within the last six weeks the Manitoba government came out with a white paper called "In Search of a Land Policy for Manitoba". In support of this paper the NDP government created a strawman in Manitoba by saying acquisition of land is so rampant in the province that land is being taken away from the farmers. This strawman was stripped during the first five minutes of a public meeting held by the farmers of Manitoba. What became very clear to them, and what has become very clear to the people of Manitoba, is that this strawman put up by the NDP government was not fear of foreign ownership but fear of government ownership of farm land.
According to their own statistics, approximately 93 per cent of all agricultural land in Manitoba is owned by Manitobans who are active farmers. The problem is that the average age of these farmers is well into the fifties, so more money must be made available to young farmers. Of the remaining 7 per cent, 4 per cent was held by Manitobans living in Brandon and Winnipeg; roughly 2 per cent was held by Canadians not resident in Manitoba; approximately one per cent of the agricultural land in Manitoba was owned by foreigners. That was their strawman,
Farm Credit Act
Madam Speaker and, as I say, it took the farmers about five minutes to figure that out. They are now asking me for more money from the Farm Credit Corporation so that they can get a loan based on business principles. They want to meet their obligations, but they do not want to compete with the government on ownership.
This very insidious plan of the Manitoba government is actually raising the price of land that farmers want to buy. For example, a farmer in my riding had made a verbal deal with another farmer to buy land at $130 an acre. A representative of the Manitoba Agricultural Credit Corporation approached this farmer, opened his little black book, and said: "We will pay you $140 an acre". So who do you think got the land, Madam Speaker? That is the kind of problem we are facing in Manitoba.
Then there was the case of a young farmer who wanted to get into farming. Here I commend the minister for the clause that allows a person to work for five years and become the eventual owner if his principal occupational activity is farming. This young man had a loan from the Manitoba Agricultural Credit Corporation, and like many young farmers he needed operating capital. He then asked for an additional loan and they told him to come back two days later, which he did. They then told him, "We think you should double the amount you have asked us for, but we will buy your land. We will take the equity you have in your land at the present time and then we will give you your operating capital". Then five years later he has an option to buy it back, but during this five years he leases it, pays for it under the leasing arrangement, and pays the property tax. At the end of the five years he pays the total accumulated tax or interest. On top of that he has to finance any improvements he makes on the land within the five years.
In conclusion, I agree with the minister-though I sometimes feel he exaggerates his own importance in this matter-that we have a moral obligation as Canadians to increase food production. There is a starving world out there. As I have said on many occasions, we cannot expect the farmers to finance the surplus. But let us get more money to our young farmers and avoid land ownership by government which takes land out of production and too often increases the price of food and land in Canada. To my way of thinking this is entirely contrary to the personal incentives that have built up rural Canada.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

speechtext:
I did hope that my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), would be here to assist me today as he is very fluent in the Gaelic language.
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
The Cape Breton Development Corporation has shown a great deal of leadership, not just in programs associated with developing an economic stability on the island, but also in making residents aware of our cultural heritage. Because of this fact it would seem to me that if Devco were to give leadership in the establishment of such a centre it would find ready and willing allies in the many cultural and ethnic groups that exist now and have existed for many years in Cape Breton.
We have a long and exciting history in Cape Breton, which began with the landfall of John Cabot at Cape North in 1497. We have attracted people from almost every part of the world and of almost every ethnic extraction ever since.
Canadians of Scottish origin, like myself, take a great deal of pride in the fact that we have a very active and vigorous Gaelic Society in Cape Breton. We are also extremely proud of the Gaelic college of Celtic folk arts and highland homecrafts at St. Ann's. This college was established by the Cape Breton Island Gaelic Foundation in 1939, and it holds the unique position of being the only one in North America. It is said that Nova Scotia is the cradle of Celtic culture in the new world. Students from across Canada from every province, as well as from every state of the United States and from around the world, come to Cape Breton to study at this college as it offers courses in the Gaelic language, piping, drumming, highland dancing and weaving.
We cannot and would not want to denigrate the extremely valuable contributions made daily by the Cape Breton Folk Arts Council, the Industrial Cape Breton Multi-Cultural Association, the Irish Benevolent Society, and in the Ukrainian, Polish, Italian, Lebanese, Greek and Chinese communities, to name a few. They all actively pursue their cultural traditions which enrich our lives. Equally as important are the activities of the Black Cultural Club at Sydney Academy, and the Black United Front. The Union of Nova Scotia Indians plays an effective role too, probably because the Eskasoni Indian Reserve is the largest such reserve in the province of Nova Scotia.
It may seem strange to this House to have me say that the original coal miners of Cape Breton were from France. They came, they stayed, and they are with us today-not the same coal miners but their descendants. Their ancestors are busily engaged in promoting their culture and their language. As an example of just how long the French have been in Cape Breton and involved in coal mining let me read you an excerpt from a book entitled "First Things in Acadia":
Captain Poulet mentioned coal in Cape Breton in a report to the French king, and one vessel, La Bretonne, carried a cargo to France in 1687.
Incidentally, the first Jesuit mission in North America was located at a place, strangely enough now called Eng-lishtown, about 40 miles from my own home.
We also have the reconstruction of the Fortress of Louisburg by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. This amazing and exciting project recognizes the value of the contributions by both the French and the British in the founding of this nation. I must say that it still gives me a tremendous amount of
February 28, 1975

pleasure and personal satisfaction to have been a member of the government party when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister, as it was that administration that saw the merit in the recreation of this fortress which will be an everlasting tribute to our forefathers.
The mosaic of our cultural being is dependent upon our recognition of the history and traditions of our peoples. If we are to remain uniquely different from our United States friends we must at all times and in every way possible care for and cultivate the varied contributions that produce the inspiration for our uniqueness.
The proposed cultural centre would not only be a forum for creative expression by our ethnic and native groups, but it would also provide the incentive for a still greater development of our varied cultures that, when united, produce Canadianism, and we are all justly proud of being Canadian.
It is my hope that as a result of this debate Devco will initiate, through its able officers, a program to spearhead the establishment of a cultural centre in Cape Breton, both financially and through their leadership, so that tomorrow Cape Breton will be a better place in which to live, and so that we may all get to know each other better by learning of the customs and traditions of our neighbours. This would be of fantastic value, not just to Cape Bretoners but also to all the visitors from across this land and around the world who come to visit Cape Breton.
The suggestion that federal funds be used for a cultural centre is not new or innovative. The National Arts Centre in Ottawa and the Confederation Centre of the Arts in Charlottetown were both funded to a great degree by the federal government. It is also my understanding that public money has been used for such projects in other parts of Canada.
This month an ethnic festival was held in Sydney at which there were 12 different performing groups. A very successful evening was held. I look forward to the day when I can walk into a cultural centre in Cape Breton, dedicated to the multi-culturalism of this nation, and listen to the "Men of the Deeps", who have performed all over Canada and in the United States, comprised of coal miners of many ethnic origins.
I look forward to the day when I can watch the "Stornaway Scottish Dancers", see the "Irish Folk Dancers", hear the "Young Gaelic Singers of Big Pond", observe the "Ukrainian Dancers of Sydney" and enjoy "Lee Cremo", a Micmac fiddler or, if you wish to be a little fancier, violinist, although there is a controversy as to whether you are playing a violin when you are fiddling. In any event, Mr. Cremo is a Micmac from the Eskasoni Reserve who has appeared at international competitions across this country.
I look forward to listening to "John Allen Cameron", and I do not have to tell you who he is, and to tapping my toes to the "Cape Breton Calypso Band". Those are just a few that come to my mind, even though I realize there are numerous other extremely talented groups and individuals one might also enjoy. Maybe I would even be able to hear my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, a fluent Gaelic linguist, sing "Ho Ro Mo Nigh'n
Cultural Centre
Donn Bhodheach", literally translated "My Pretty Fair Maiden". Maybe we could open this cultural centre in the presence of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I look forward to seeing him wear his Elliott tartan kilt. I have been looking forward to that for a long time since it was presented to him, and I have not seen him wear it yet. That would be the occasion for him to wear it.
Before resuming my seat I wish to say how pleased I am to have had the opportunity of presenting this motion. I ask all hon. members present to give this matter their most careful consideration.

speechtext:
It has not, however, done very much good in my constituency because the provincial government has consistently refused to apply any of those funds to our area. In modern

society one cannot over emphasize the importance of a modern highway system, not only as a means of transportation for goods and services but also as a means to protect life and health in these days of high speed travel. When my people are suffering the effects of this deficiency, I cannot speak in favour of the allocation of federal funds for the building of cultural centres.
Today, well into 1975, we in my constituency still do not enjoy the cultural advantage of having decent television service. Indeed there are communities there which receive practically no service at all. They cannot even receive a signal. Those of us who can receive a signal have two choices: we can watch the one channel, which is obsolete in its equipment, or we can watch nothing. For ten years we have been fighting for an alternate service, and we are always told that it is a question of money. However, it has never been suggested that we be given in our area a lower rate schedule in our income tax to compensate for the services denied us but which other parts of Canada take for granted. I cannot support financial outlays for cultural centres when my people have such primitive television service. We do not even have access, for instance, to FM radio.
Our economy depends on a base in which there is far too little diversification. It is predicated almost entirely on the exploitation of natural resources, either from land or sea. Almost without exception our precious resources are being shipped from our midst in a raw or semi-manufactured state. Why should this be so? Do we not have the talent and ingenuity to carry out these labour intensive stages in the utilization of our natural resources? Must we look forward forever to being providers of raw materials and buying finished products back to keep foreign and upper Canadian industrial wheels turning? I cannot agree to funding cultural centres while we do not have all the opportunities for employment we require.
Only last week I learned of a rather drastic cutback in the number of armed forces personnel stationed at CFB Chatham. For some areas of Canada this might seem an insignificant development, but for our area it is a real economic blow because our small service industry is very much dependent on these people as customers. When we have so delicate an economy that the transfer of 200 military personnel is a serious matter, we must get to work to develop that base upon which we depend for all our physical needs.
We hear a great deal about the Atlantic fishery from time to time. I know our Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) is keenly aware of our problems and is actively seeking solutions to them. But a rationalization of the Atlantic fishery is a far higher priority to me than the establishment of additional cultural centres. If there are any extra federal dollars floating around let us put them where they would provide the basic necessities of life. Then we can look after our cultural heritage.

speechtext:
No trouble at all-can you? Much is said about freedom, and I subscribe to the view that we live in the most free society on this earth. I submit to you and to this honourable House, however, that as long as there are festering sores of economic disparity on the body politic, the national spirit cannot be truly free. While any person is enslaved to a life of drudgery to earn his daily bread, his spirit enjoys no freedom.
Atlantic Canada is the oldest and, in many senses, the richest part of this great nation. We have given much to the building of this new nation in social, cultural, spiritual, political and economic terms. We appreciate the efforts of recent federal governments to close the economic gap, and the present government has done more than any other. We also need the equalization grants and the efforts of DREE, but we must continue our efforts-indeed we must re-dedicate ourselves to the eradication of the disparities of which I have spoken. To do that we must keep our priorities in proper perspective. We cannot afford at this time to dilute our efforts toward the development of a

sound, diversified and stable economy. If we do, we shall soon find ourselves wallowing in a sea of confusion surrounded by lost opportunities and broken hope.
If we lose our perspective, if we fail to order our priorities, if we spend our federal grants on social and cultural frills, we shall have betrayed our trust and subjected future generations to the same economic hardships through which the present and many generations of our Atlantic fellows have so steadfastly laboured.
I hope the hon. gentleman gets his cultural centre at some future time, Madam Speaker, but in my opinion it is the wrong project at the wrong time. As Marie Antoinette learned to her sorrow, you must not feed the people cake when they have no bread.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can understand a member from the maritime provinces, or indeed from the Atlantic provinces complaining about economic conditions in that part of Canada. I confess, however, that I find it a bit strange to hear a Liberal member doing this without realizing that in effect he is making the point that the federal government for far too long has failed to meet the needs of Atlantic Canada.
To suggest that because not enough has been done for the economy of the Atlantic provinces, for the unemployed, for the fishing industry of that area, for the various needs of the people, is a reason for not spending a few dollars on culture is more than I can understand.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne)-I do not think I am doing him an injustice by repeating these words-complained about money being spent on frills, instead of on basic necessities. Good heavens, that is what the government has been doing for years all across Canada-spending money on all kinds of things that are not necessary, when basic needs like old age pensions, health services, housing and adequate employment are not being met. I did not object to the points the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi raised. I did not raise any point of order. I am surprised that he is not aware how completely out of touch he is with the shortcomings of the government which he supports.
I shall speak for only a few more minutes. I support the motion presented by the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir). I am as anxious as anyone, perhaps more anxious than many in this House, for dollars to be spent in places where they are needed, particularly in the field of old age pensions and other forms of social security. But, if I may quote my hon. friend who spoke on the point of order a moment ago, man shall not live by bread alone. I suggest that the concern for preserving the various cultures of an area like Cape Breton Island is a concern that this House does well to consider.
I am not as familiar with Cape Breton Island as I am with other parts of Nova Scotia, but I know enough of that island and I know enough of Nova Scotia to know that small as that province is, it is a place of many cultures. As

one travels, for example, along the south shore from Halifax to Yarmouth, one moves within a very few miles from one type of culture to another.
My own people happened to live for a couple of hundred years in Barrington township, which is a little bit of puritan New England. To the east of Barrington township one runs into Shelburne, an intensely Loyalist area. Going further east, along the south shore you come to an area where the background is German. Going the other way you come to Tusket and Argyle, to Yarmouth and then on Digby. In each of these areas there are different cultures that make up the great province of Nova Scotia.
I believe that anything which helps the people of that province to preserve those cultures is all to the good. I should like to see the same kind of thing done on the mainland. Of course we who descend from the mainland of Nova Scotia have always had a problem trying to persuade the Cape Bretoners that there is a mainland. In any case, this is a good start and I am happy to give my support to this excellent motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to join in this debate and I support most heartily the motion before the House.
Having heard the kind speech of the distinguished and senior member, I am prompted to use the Gaelic phrase, Is shin uilig shin, and then move on to something else, because he said just about everything a member of parliament should say on the subject. I approve his emphasis on the multicultural background of Cape Breton, that place which we generous Prince Edward Islanders salute as the other island, an island of beauty and history.
Since biblical expressions seem to be in vogue this afternoon, this being Friday afternoon, such as that man does not live by bread alone, I must point out, of course, that we must live by bread. As a supporter of the government which did something about Louisburg Fortress and dealt with other vital issues by establishing the road to resources program and Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, let me say that, for those reasons, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is and always will be very popular in the Atlantic region.
The hon. member who moved the motion spoke about cultural centres already established. May I say how very much the life of Prince Edward Island has been enriched by the Confederation Centre of the Performing Arts which was built with the assistance of the governments and the people of all provinces, and with the assistance of the federal government. The centre has added greatly to our cultural heritage and to the quality of our lives, and we cherish it. We regard it as a wonderful memorial to Charlottetown's finest hour, that day in 1864 when that beautiful city hosted the meeting of the Fathers of Confederation, from which sprang this parliament and this dominion.
If the hon. member had confined himself to just one of the great cultural ingredients of the area-I believe he excluded the English, although there are a few English in Cape Breton; I was not upset by the omission-he would still have talked about a tradition worthy of preservation. One of the greatest honours done me was when I was invited to speak to the Gaelic mod at St. Ann's, Cape
February 28, 1975

Breton Island. I was introduced by my colleague who moved this motion. I ran into a certain hard aspect of the Scottish heritage. I had checked out of my motel, near St. Ann's. As I was to be guest speaker I had assumed that I would be put up at St. Ann's, but my assumption proved ill founded. I discovered that no such thing was contemplated and I had to. hustle back to my hotel where I was lucky enough to be given a room. Clearly, Scottish frugality has not left the people of Prince Edward Island or of Cape Breton.
That any member from the Maritimes should find this motion not acceptable is beyond comprehension. After all, because of confederation-and we knew from the beginning that this might be so-we have been deprived of many commercial and economic advantages which are available to the larger community of which we are proud to be one part. In many ways we have grown accustomed to economic disadvantage. But that, surely, is no reason for someone to suggest that we should cut down on our cultural aspects of life. Even though the great and perhaps lamented Walter Gordon suggested, when a royal commissioner, that Maritimers might be better off moving out of the area and looking for jobs elsewhere, he saw a certain quality of life down there. This motion seeks to preserve that, and to honour and enlarge the cultural contribution which has been made by that fine and beautiful part of Canada.
Hon. members can visit Prince Edward Island on their summer holidays and then take the Wood Island ferry to Nova Scotia and visit the mover of this motion. I am sure that they will receive fine hospitality in both these fine communities.
Nova Scotia has produced some good men. Some of our greatest men have come from Cape Breton. I suppose every one of us can think of the four great public men who have come from Nova Scotia. They are Joseph Howe, Charles Tupper, Angus L. Macdonald and Robert Stanfield. The one who came from Cape Breton was a man of great presence, great charm and great wisdom. I remember two things about Angus L. Macdonald, which gladden my heart. When Ramsay Macdonald, the Prime Minister of Britain, came to Halifax on his way to Washington, he was greeted by Angus Macdonald in Gaelic; but the man from Scotland did not know a word of Gaelic although the man from Cape Breton knew it well. I do not think there is much wrong with a man who was too busy in Canada to attend the coronation of the King in London but who, a couple of months later, found it possible to spend three weeks at a Gaelic mod in Edinburgh.

We can support members like my colleague who has directed us to some of the important things, things which will last longer than the most sturdily built road or the best constructed building, things of the heart, things of the spirit.
This is an area in which Canada has been far, far too reluctant to move. We have allowed things to leave the country. We have allowed historic buildings to be
Cultural Centre
destroyed. It has only been a matter of two or three years since we did not do a thing when the beautiful home of Sir Robert Borden, which he occupied for a whole generation, was torn down and apartment blocks put up in its place.
All across this country we find that historic sites have been wrecked, ruined and forgotten. Any move that this parliament makes to support the people who are interested in the heritage of Canada, who want to enrich our cultural appreciation and enlarge our historic dimension, people like the mover of this motion, should not be condemned. They should not be cast aside for not building roads or not bringing in enough bread and butter, but hailed as men of the future, men who can see these things which are eternal and significant in this great country of ours.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I wish to enter this discussion briefly, not to make any pronouncement on what is needed most, a Cape Breton cultural centre or better roads, but in the broader concept of the cultural concerns and some of the things that I hope, if and when the cultural centre proposed by the hon. member goes forward, might be included in it.
What the hon. member is proposing is important now and will be much more important in the future. More and more Canada will be depending upon immigration for its population growth. Each one who comes to our shores will bring a new type of culture, a culture that every Canadian wants to see preserved, one which can be shared in a very real and meaningful way.
I agree wholeheartedly with the previous speaker who said thank goodness that at this point in time we are starting to have some appreciation of our culture and heritage. I have a particularly strong feeling about preserving heritage, our old buildings and old customs. Anything that adds support to this certainly should be commended.
I wish the mover of the motion had expanded a bit in terms of the concept of the cultural centre he was talking about. I am not entirely clear in terms of what conditions he might have on it. I would like to put forward my one concern in terms of the motion. It is really one that I spoke of in a debate during private members' hour last week. I refer to the role of crown corporations financing many concepts for which they are not really charged with the basic responsibility.
I am not totally knowledgeable, or even as knowledgeable as I should be with regard to the terms of reference of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. It may very well be within their jurisdiction that such a cultural centre would be something justifiable not only to finance but to operate and promote. If it should not be, I would have some concern about whether that should be the vehicle the hon. member would be promoting to bring this about. If it is not within their terms of reference, there must be other government departments, approaches or avenues that would be more concerned.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I thank the hon. member for his comments. I am enjoying what he is saying. Just to clarify the situation, it is indeed that. They have engaged in the promotion of culture in a small way so far.

Cultural Centre

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CULTURAL CENTRE
speechtext:
I think it is good that communities set up cultural centres, a place where people of various cultures and backgrounds can meet with each other and share their respective cultural heritages, working together for a better understanding of Canada's heritage.
In my constituency there are many different ethnic groups and cultural backgrounds. While I think it is a good approach to have a cultural centre such as this, we should be very careful that each group has a facility to keep its own culture and promote that, as opposed to having a large cultural centre which pressures cultural groups to blend together, perhaps losing some of the distinctive things we strive most to preserve.
In terms of the broader context of establishing cultural centres across the country, there are three needs. One is to preserve traditional customs and heritages. The second is really a language situation and the third is an educational centre for the benefit of people coming to this country.
As this is International Women's Year any cultural centre should be very attuned to the role of woman. That has not always been done. We tend to structure programs and so on to the benefit of the male. I feel that this year we should recognize this as an objective.
A cultural centre should not be the be all and end all. One of the very great strengths of this type of approach would be if a cultural centre had an extension program to reach out into the community and make its presence known. By that I mean a very large community in terms of the cultural needs they are preserving, the arts and crafts they are promoting.
Judging by many of the facilities which are perhaps not as large in scope as the hon. member is talking about, perhaps the ethnic group that originally promoted it, that knows about it and that uses it is not as large a factor in the community as it could be. An active promotional outreaching program should be a part of this.
Perhaps the hon. member is aware that in the city of Toronto there is an annual caravan program that is really a promotional program on behalf of each of the cultural and ethnic groups in the city. They invite the rest of the community to share that with them. It is a very successful program. It is the type of program that should be part of any cultural establishment or program.
Something that is perhaps apropos of what the hon. member mentions is that in many areas of the country new Canadians have great difficulty adapting to Canadian society. One of the greatest problems facing new Canadians is often an acquisition of basic skills in one or other of the official languages, whether English or French.
There is an active group in my own riding which spends a great deal of time helping immigrants to our shores to acquire language skills. One handicap often faced in such efforts is the lack of suitable facilities, the halls which are available are simply not suited to these purposes. This is an effort which is surely deserving of encouragement. I am sure the hon. member would agree, though, that close co-operation with provincial legislatures is required in this connection since we are dealing with an aspect of education, and every care must be taken to reflect the

priorities and intentions of the provincial government involved.
The government services provided for new Canadians are badly needed, but we should remember that it is a long walk for these new arrivals to go to some of the official offices and talk about the things which concern them. I hope we might be able to establish centres of a type where these people could feel more at home in the presence of people at the official level who spoke their language and shared their traditions.
Many of us are concerned about the large numbers of immigrants who have come to Canada in the last 15 years or so and have not yet taken out citizenship. If citizenship judges were able to attend in centres such as I have described, it is probable that more immigrants would take advantage of the opportunity to become Canadians. We are all concerned, too, about manpower training and the upgrading of technical skills. It is possible that this work, also, could be carried out in such centres.
I am wholeheartedly in support of measures to preserve the customs and traditions which enrich our cultural heritage, and I approve the setting up of facilities where people from both sides of the border can share this inheritance. I hope that in due course a facility of this type will be built on Cape Breton Island.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe my hon. friend from Cape Breton-The Sydneys has contributed a great cultural event to a day which has been concerned with other things. It is very important that the movement he is attempting in Cape Breton should have the support of all members of the House as a matter of principle. We are looking at cultures which because of neglect, because of abuse, because of wrong headedness will soon be classed as endangered species.
When we consider cultural centres we might consider a cultural centre in the middle of Montreal because of the difficulty those who want to know the English language culture in Quebec are experiencing with respect to Bill 22. There will be an opportunity to debate that matter at some other time. It is heartening to know that we are so mature in Canada as to be mindful of the traditions of the past, traditions of excellence in literature, the arts and all the other things that made up our past. There is something worth saving. There was a society created in the early days of our history which is worth remembering and worth building upon. That is why, all over the country, buildings are being preserved, works of art are being dusted off, old ways are being revived.
In my own Township of Nepean in the riding of Grenville-Carleton we are now considering the establishment of a cultural centre, and I hope this will be representative of not just the two main cultures in Canada but of the many cultures which make this country so rich. I hope this will still the fives that emphasize only two cultures in this country and which are injuring the unity of confederation.
I congratulate my hon. friend for emphasizing this concept, one which ought to be followed in every area of the country.

Madam Speaker, I read the motion of my hon. colleague and I
February 28, 1975

agree with his suggestion although I doubt he has chosen the proper means of achieving his objective. What I mean is that the Canadian Secretariat of State already has a national policy on museums which, to my mind, could achieve the purpose of my colleague, that is, to set up a cultural centre on Cape Breton island.
Indeed, that museum policy, as announced in 1972 by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), indicates clearly that in that year a credit of $750,000 was provided for local exhibition centres that would offer, to the public, travelling exhibits coming from larger museums or the national loan collection.
Government communiques stipulated that the national exhibition centres had to be maintained by members of the communities they served, therefore, by native communities where they were to be established. Most of them should be set up in community centres or city halls which would but rarely have collections. They will feature mobile exhibitions composed of pieces from either important collections or the national loan collection created under this new policy.
Madam Speaker, I think my colleague should be invited to make his request under the program of the Secretary of State of Canada. In my opinion, we undoubtedly have

programs meeting the cultural objectives that I support and my colleague has set forth in the proposal whose contents we are debating this afternoon.
